title: The law where the raise climbs with the rank
intro: A commissioned post is the exception the Constitution carves out of the public-exam rule: whoever holds one sat no exam, and can be appointed and dismissed at any moment. On 2 June 2025 a law raised the entire table of these posts in the federal Executive, in two instalments. The raise was not the same for everyone, and it did not vary gradually: there are four steps — 30%, 23%, 17% and 9% — and which step you get depends only on how senior the post is.
law.where: Annex CCXCVII, item f — which becomes Annex I of Law 11.526 of 4 October 2007
gap.title: The same raise, in reais per month
gap.topLabel: more per month at the top of the table
gap.bottomLabel: more per month at the bottom of it
gap.note: Both figures come from the same table, the same law and the same eleven-month window. This is not a comparison between different careers or different years: it is the difference between the first line and the last line of a single annex. One detail of the table, so no one has to check later: of the thirteen bottom levels, twelve got exactly 9% and CCE-9 got 8.50%.
fce.title: And there are two columns, not one
fce.body: Every line of the table carries two values: the post (CCE) and the function (FCE). The function can only be held by someone who is already a civil servant. From CCE-5 up, it is worth exactly 60% of the post. From CCE-4 down, the two are worth the same. Which means the difference in money between being a career servant and being appointed from outside exists only in the fourteen levels at the top.
minimumWage.title: An outside ruler, over the same window
minimumWage.body: The minimum wage went from R$ 1,518 on 1 January 2025 to R$ 1,621 on 1 January 2026: a raise of 6.79%. Over the same window, the bottom of the commissioned-post table rose 9% and the top rose 30%.
minimumWage.source: Planalto — the decree raising the minimum wage to R$ 1,621
question: The inflation eating the pay of whoever holds a CCE-1 is the same inflation eating the pay of whoever holds a CCE-18. Why, then, did one of them get R$ 35 more a month and the other R$ 7,365?
